questions.question: Let $A$ be a real $n\times n$ matrix with eigenvalue $\lambda$ and eigenvector $\boldsymbol{p}\in\mathbb{C}^n$. Conjugating $A\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda\boldsymbol{p}$ entrywise gives $\bar{A}\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}=\bar\lambda\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}$. Which fact turns this into the statement that $\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ for $\bar\lambda$?
options: $\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}=\boldsymbol{p}$, because eigenvectors can be scaled to be real.
$\bar\lambda=\lambda$, because eigenvalues of real matrices are real numbers.
$\bar{A}=A$, because every entry of $A$ is real.

questions.question: Let $A$ be a real $n\times n$ matrix and $\lambda=a+b\mathrm{i}$ with $b\ne0$ an eigenvalue of $A$. Can a nonzero vector $\boldsymbol{p}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ with only real entries satisfy $A\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda\boldsymbol{p}$?
options: Yes: the real part of any complex eigenvector is itself a real eigenvector.
Yes, but only when $\lvert\lambda\rvert=1$, as for a rotation matrix.
No, but only because $A$ must then be singular with $\det A=0$.
No: $A\boldsymbol{p}$ would be real while $\lambda\boldsymbol{p}$ has a nonreal entry.

questions.question: Let $A$ be a real $5\times5$ matrix, and count its eigenvalues with algebraic multiplicity, so there are five in total. What must be true about its real eigenvalues?
options: All five eigenvalues are real, because the entries of $A$ are real.
No eigenvalue need be real; all five may be nonreal numbers.
Exactly one eigenvalue is real; the other four always form two pairs.
At least one eigenvalue is real, because the nonreal ones pair up.

questions.question: Let $A$ be a real $6\times6$ matrix for which $1+2\mathrm{i}$ is an eigenvalue of algebraic multiplicity $2$. What is the algebraic multiplicity of $1-2\mathrm{i}$ as an eigenvalue of $A$?
options: Exactly $1$, since the conjugate is added only once.
At least $1$, but it cannot be determined further.
Exactly $2$, the same as that of $1+2\mathrm{i}$.
Exactly $4$, so that the total count is even.

questions.question: The rotation matrix $R_\theta=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $\mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\theta}$. For which angles $\theta$ are these a pair of nonreal conjugate eigenvalues?
options: Exactly when $\theta$ is not an integer multiple of $\pi$.
Exactly when $\theta$ is not an integer multiple of $2\pi$.
Exactly when $\theta$ is not an integer multiple of $\pi/2$.
For every $\theta$, since a rotation never has real eigenvalues.

questions.question: For the real matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&-5\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, compute the eigenvalues from the characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2-(\operatorname{tr}A)\lambda+\det A$. Which are they?

The real matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&-2\\4&-1\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalue $1+2\mathrm{i}$ with eigenvector $\boldsymbol{p}=(1,\,1-\mathrm{i})^{\top}$. Which vector is an eigenvector of $A$ for the eigenvalue $1-2\mathrm{i}$?
A real $2\times2$ matrix $A$ has eigenvalue $-1+2\mathrm{i}$. Which polynomial is the characteristic polynomial $\det(A-\lambda I)$ of $A$?

A real $2\times2$ matrix $A$ has eigenvalues $1\pm\mathrm{i}$. Using that $A\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda\boldsymbol{p}$ implies $A^4\boldsymbol{p}=\lambda^4\boldsymbol{p}$, which are the eigenvalues of $A^4$?
A real matrix $A$ has the eigenvalue $\lambda=0.5+0.9\mathrm{i}$. What happens to the powers $\lambda^t$ as $t\to\infty$, $t=1,2,\dots$?
options: $\lambda^t\to0$, since its real part $0.5$ lies below $1$.
$\lambda^t\to0$, since both parts $0.5$ and $0.9$ lie below $1$.
$\lambda^t$ keeps modulus $1$, since a nonreal $\lambda$ only rotates.

questions.question: A real $4\times4$ matrix $A$ is known to have the eigenvalues $1+\mathrm{i}$ and $2\mathrm{i}$. What can be concluded about the list of all eigenvalues of $A$, counted with algebraic multiplicity?
options: It contains $1\pm\mathrm{i}$ and $2\mathrm{i}$, plus one unknown real eigenvalue.
It contains $1+\mathrm{i}$ and $2\mathrm{i}$, plus two unknown real eigenvalues.
It contains $1\pm\mathrm{i}$ and $\pm2\mathrm{i}$, but their multiplicities are open.

questions.question: For a real $2\times2$ matrix $A$, how is the condition $\det A>0$ related to the statement that $A$ has a pair of nonreal conjugate eigenvalues?
options: It is necessary but not sufficient, as $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ shows.
It is sufficient but not necessary, as $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ shows.
It is necessary and sufficient, because $\det A=\lambda\bar\lambda>0$.
It is neither, as $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ with $\det A=-1$ shows.

questions.question: A real $3\times3$ matrix $A$ has eigenvalue $1+2\mathrm{i}$ and trace $\operatorname{tr}A=5$. Using that the trace is the sum and the determinant the product of the eigenvalues, what is $\det A$?

The real matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&\sqrt{3}\\-\sqrt{3}&1\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $1\pm\sqrt{3}\,\mathrm{i}$. Writing them as $\rho \mathrm{e}^{\pm\mathrm{i}\theta}$, by which factor $\rho$ does $A$ scale and through which angle $\lvert\theta\rvert$ does it rotate per application?

The real matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&0\\1&2&0\\0&0&5\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalue $2+\mathrm{i}$ with eigenvector $\boldsymbol{p}=(1,-\mathrm{i},0)^{\top}=\boldsymbol{u}+\mathrm{i}\boldsymbol{w}$, $\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{w}$ real. On which real subspace does $A$ act, for the pair $2\pm\mathrm{i}$, as a rotation through a nonzero angle combined with a scaling?
options: The line spanned by $(0,0,1)^{\top}$, the real eigenvector

questions.question: The proposition that $\bar\lambda$ is an eigenvalue whenever $\lambda$ is assumes that the square matrix is real. Which matrix shows that this hypothesis cannot be dropped?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, with eigenvalue $\mathrm{i}$ but no real eigenvector
$\begin{pmatrix}1&\mathrm{i}\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, a complex matrix whose eigenvalue $1$ is real

questions.question: A real matrix $A$ has eigenvalue $\lambda=a+b\mathrm{i}$, $b\ne0$, with eigenvector $\boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{u}+\mathrm{i}\boldsymbol{w}$, $\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{w}$ real. Why must $\boldsymbol{u}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$ be linearly independent?
options: Because $\boldsymbol{u}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$ are eigenvectors of $A$ for the two different eigenvalues $a$ and $b$.
Because $\boldsymbol{p}$ and $\bar{\boldsymbol{p}}$ are always orthogonal, so their real and imaginary parts are as well.
Because $\det A\ge a^2+b^2>0$ makes $A$ invertible, and invertible maps keep vectors independent.
Otherwise $\boldsymbol{p}$ is a complex multiple of one real vector, which would then be a real eigenvector for $\lambda$.

questions.question: The real matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ has $\operatorname{tr}A=-1$ and $\det A=1$. Using its eigenvalues in polar form, what is the smallest integer $t\ge1$ with $A^t=I$?
options: No such $t$ exists, since the eigenvalues are nonreal

questions.question: A real matrix $A$ has eigenvalue $a+b\mathrm{i}$ ($b\ne0$) with eigenvector $\boldsymbol{p}=\boldsymbol{u}+\mathrm{i}\boldsymbol{w}$, where $\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{w}$ are real vectors. Comparing real parts in $A\boldsymbol{p}=(a+b\mathrm{i})\boldsymbol{p}$, what is $A\boldsymbol{u}$?
For the real matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&k\\-2&3\end{pmatrix}$ with real parameter $k$, for which values of $k$ does $A$ have a pair of nonreal conjugate eigenvalues?
